The authors propose a very low sturdy dressing stool once sitting steadily, with feet flat, and standing diaper changes for a baby who stands and resists lying down.
The authors suggest consistent places for toothbrush and mirror before independent use, and a potty when interest appears; they note some babies are interested around 12 months and others much later.

The authors advise avoiding screens before two and little or none after two, describing sensory exploration as preferable to passive fast-changing screen entertainment.
The authors include adult demands to perform on cue among obstacles and suggest observing instead of testing a baby’s skills.
The authors encourage language and opportunities that do not restrict children by gender or define them by a temporary struggle.
The authors suggest naming what the baby points to, peekaboo, and sound-location play with familiar sounds from different places.
The language observation list invites noticing the baby’s responses, voice, gestures and changing interests before adjusting support.
The authors describe increasingly independent standing and walking, with the baby choosing when to release support.
Once cruising is becoming efficient, the authors describe a push wagon the baby can approach, pull up on and push independently.
The authors describe a large stable ball tracker for pulling up, dropping a ball, bending to retrieve and repeating.
The authors describe supervised stair exploration and climbing equipment as babies become interested in climbing.
The authors suggest pliable materials for hand/thumb use, including play dough, tissue tearing and squeezable bath toys.
As babies become steadier on their feet, the authors suggest an accessible drawer containing items the adult is comfortable having emptied.

The authors’ Stair row: Three low wide stairs with handrail at either end of a bridge offer movement.
The authors’ Ball tracker row: Small ball enters top of framed ramps and drops through successive end holes; row names visual/auditory tracking and movement.
The authors’ Spinning top row: A tin top with pump handle invites following its movement; later the baby can operate it.
The authors’ Box with drawer and ball row: Top posting hole and pull-out drawer support intentional release and finding the ball again.
The authors’ Box with knitted ball row: A square box has a hole slightly smaller than the knitted ball and a drawer, for posting and recovery.
The authors’ Box with balls to push row: Rectangular box with three top holes/balls supports pushing/posting and intentional release.
The authors’ Wagon row: Wagon heavy enough not to tip when child pulls up; source suggests a sandbag for weighting.
The authors’ Cabinet doors and drawers row: Adult places room-appropriate objects in cupboards/drawers, e.g. plastic kitchenware or hairbrushes/clips in a bathroom drawer, for discovery.
